summary:
Sachsen-Anhalt stands under the German national framework: federal constitutional and equality protections apply in every Land, identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove that floor. Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 without press coverage.

The case that now drives policy in this Land is Marla-Svenja Liebich's. In July 2023 the Halle District Court sentenced her to one year and six months' imprisonment without parole for incitement to hatred, defamation and insult. At the end of 2024 she changed her legal gender from male to female by declaration at a registry office under the federal Self-Determination Act, and the chief public prosecutor in Halle told MDR Sachsen-Anhalt that she would begin the term at Chemnitz women's prison. German outlets including Der Spiegel questioned the seriousness of the change.

Placement went the other way. DW reported on 16 July 2026 that Liebich, legally registered as a woman since 2025, was transferred to a men's prison at Zeithain in the Meissen district after her extradition from the Czech Republic, where she had been arrested in April 2026. Prison management said the decision prioritised the safety of women at the Chemnitz facility, while critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law. A court has yet to decide whether the changes can be reversed, so the outcome of the central question is unresolved.

Sachsen-Anhalt is one of three Länder, with Sachsen and Thüringen, pressing a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. The dpa report of 2 June 2026 describes a proposed abuse review mechanism allowing registry-office intervention on objective, documentable grounds, triggered by the Liebich case and backed by Union MPs, resisted by the SPD, while the federal family ministry runs a scheduled evaluation of the Act.

Legal gender recognition itself is straightforward on paper: adults change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice, a procedure in force since 1 November 2024 that replaced the Transsexuals Act of 1980. Entry and document checks are therefore unlikely to raise an issue for a visitor carrying consistent papers. A visitor who is arrested or held in Sachsen-Anhalt, by contrast, faces the same binary housing rule that produced the Zeithain transfer.
tangentialFactors:
Direction among the Länder differs. Sachsen-Anhalt, Sachsen and Thüringen are moving to restrict the self-declaration route, while Rhineland-Palatinate inserted a new § 17 into its prison act on 1 March 2026 to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and the Berlin prison service publishes an information page for trans people in custody setting out rules and contacts across the city's facilities. A visitor's placement outcome therefore depends on where in Germany custody occurs.

Screening at airports has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, telling Resident Advisor in June 2025 that officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she gave the publication a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected spaces in the leisure sector has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off public argument over registered trans women's access, and months of debate followed over fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Media framing in the Liebich reporting has been hostile in places: Der Spiegel and other outlets questioned the sincerity of her gender change, and coverage characterised the change as an abuse of the law, which is the framing the Sachsen-Anhalt initiative rests on. She also lost a case against the journalist Julian Reichelt at Berlin Regional Court.
localsOnly:
Residents who wish to change their legal gender do so under the Self-Determination Act by giving three months' notice to the registry office, a procedure in force since 1 November 2024. The 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019 under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status and was clarified in April 2019 as applying to intersex people only, not transgender people.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and in education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection.

Since May 2020 a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has carried penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment. The German STOP the HATE campaign runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people. Sachsen-Anhalt residents with family or community ties to those schemes are affected by that decision.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses Sachsen-Anhalt's own correctional act or its provisions on the housing of trans prisoners, so the Lower Saxony § 170(2) reading cannot be confirmed as the rule applied inside this Land. Practice in Sachsen-Anhalt prisons at intake, including whether placement corresponding to gender identity is granted exceptionally here, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The outcome of the Liebich reversal proceedings is pending; whether her legal gender changes can be undone was undecided as of the 16 July 2026 reporting.

As of the dpa report of 2 June 2026 the Bundesrat initiative was under discussion, resisted by the SPD and running alongside a scheduled federal family ministry evaluation of the Self-Determination Act. Whether any tightening passes, and in what form, is unresolved.

No source documents enforcement outcomes for General Act on Equal Treatment claims in Sachsen-Anhalt, nor any recorded hate-crime conviction data for the Land. The airport screening complaint concerns Frankfurt Airport in Hesse and is used here as evidence of screening practice at German airports generally, not as a Sachsen-Anhalt finding.
